h: Gyanesh Kumar's burden: kill the snake without breaking the stick
dek: Harish Khare argues that the Chief Election Commissioner is now weighing on the Prime Minister's own standing, and that a Supreme Court remark could be one way out of this deadlock.
body: Harish Khare, former editor-in-chief of The Tribune, begins with an old story. In 1975 Henry Kissinger joked that he had come to save Israel's Prime Minister from his own defence minister. According to Khare, India too has had such moments, when a leader's closest people led him down the wrong road: the attempt at a deal with China in Nehru's time, Sanjay Gandhi during the Emergency, Advani at the Agra summit.

Today the situation is more dangerous, because the institutions that once held such a crisis in check have grown weak. On one side is a Prime Minister surrounded by hardline advisers; on the other, an Election Commission suspected of serving the ruling party, an opposition whose leader has nothing to lose, and an angry street movement with no leader.

Khare writes that from July to October, the power of the state stood facing unarmed young people on Delhi's streets. The Delhi Police, which answers to the Centre, did not even care about the Supreme Court's directions. He warns that if the deadlock drags on, both the disregard for court orders and the reliance on violent gangs will grow.

The writer charges that Gyanesh Kumar has dealt the institution a deep wound, and that the legal shield he has been given itself points to careful planning. Only Parliament can remove him, through impeachment, and the ruling party will not let that happen. But Khare reminds us that if the government wants, getting a resignation is not hard for it, as was seen when a Vice President stepped down in the name of 'health'.

His suggestion is that the Supreme Court cannot suspend the Commissioner, but it can make strong remarks on his conduct. That would give the Prime Minister an excuse to send Kumar off while saving face, give the opposition confidence that elections are not being stolen, and save the elections too. In other words, the snake dies and the stick does not break.
nazar: Khare's remedy is written in the language of the corridors of power, where the question is how to save the Prime Minister's honour. But for the young people sitting on the street, the question is bigger than one officer's exit: the crores of names that were cut must come back, and the law that picks the Commission must change.

Still, the article's real point is right. When the road through Parliament is shut and the courts keep putting things off, every breath of democracy comes to rest on pressure from the street. If the court truly speaks, let it speak not to save anyone's honour, but for the voter's right.
sawal: Will one Commissioner's exit bring back trust in elections?
ref: Impeachment
The process for removing the Chief Election Commissioner, which is like removing a Supreme Court judge. It needs a special majority in both Houses of Parliament.
India Cable
A newsletter by Harish Khare and other senior journalists, where this article first appeared before The Wire republished it.

h: As the people's fear fell, the regime grew more frightening
dek: Ashok Vajpeyi says that deploying more than thirty thousand personnel against unarmed young people in Delhi is proof of the government's panic, not its strength.
body: In his weekly column 'Kabhi-Kabhar' (Now and Then), Ashok Vajpeyi shows an upside-down picture this time. According to him, what happened in Delhi against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar featured a frightened state and fearless young people. In his view, this protest proved true not the power of the state but democracy itself.

The writer reminds us that more than thirty thousand security personnel were sent out against a non-violent movement. He claims that never before in free India had such a large arrangement been made against a protest, and that its aim was to scare people and throw the city's life into disorder. Yet despite the barriers and police excesses, the young people stayed calm and set up many Jantar Mantars all over Delhi.

Vajpeyi sees the biggest thing about this movement as the fact that it is mostly led by unknown young people, and that they are reviving the constitutional language of justice, equality, liberty and fraternity. They are turning a public debate full of caste, religion, hate and lies in another direction. According to the writer, the media that tried to make it look small has lost even more of what little credibility it had left.

He also says the government has openly ignored the Supreme Court's directions, and that the court's constitutional judgment will now be tested in the cases about the Election Commission. In the second part of the column, through Neera Chandhoke's book 'Languages of Freedom', he reminds us that the freedom struggle was also fought in cinema, in progressive Urdu poetry and in the theatre of IPTA, and that hero worship is like pawning the citizen's freedom. At the end comes Joy Goswami's poem 'Shasak Ke Prati' (To the Ruler), which mocks power in the voice of subjects bowed before its orders.
nazar: The most important part of Vajpeyi's point is that the scale of repression is really the scale of the state's fear. Those whose names were cut from the voter list are mostly poor, migrants and minorities, and the young people who have taken to the street for them are saying that citizenship is not a favour handed out by some office. The question is whether the court will be as fearless as these young people.
sawal: How strong is a state that is afraid of unarmed young people?
ref: IPTA
The Indian People's Theatre Association, a progressive theatre movement formed in 1943 that tied plays and songs to the people's struggles.
Kabhi-Kabhar
Ashok Vajpeyi's long-running weekly column, where literature, art and politics move side by side.

h: The institutions have bowed; now democracy will be decided on the street
dek: CPI(ML) general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya charges that in the name of the SIR, Forms 6 and 7 were turned into tools of mass exclusion.
body: Dipankar Bhattacharya begins his article on 2 October, when young people across the country chose the path of non-violent protest on Gandhi Jayanti. In Delhi, Jantar Mantar was sealed off and everyone from students to the elderly was detained. According to him, the young people brought Gandhi's method back to life, while the government answered civil disobedience with colonial-style force.

The writer lists the movement's three demands: Gyanesh Kumar's immediate resignation, the complete cancellation of the SIR, and the return of rights to voters who were wrongly removed. He recalls the 2023 law that tilted the selection of commissioners in the government's favour and gave them lifelong legal protection. Citing reports in the Indian Express, he says two commissioners recorded objections fourteen times in ten months.

His sharpest charge concerns the forms. According to him, more than thirteen crore names were cut, and the Commission is now covering this up by calling them 'missed' voters. Form 6 is meant for new voters, yet those whose names were cut are being made to fill it, which he considers illegal. Bundles of pre-filled Form 7s were caught, and the writer charges that the targets were Muslims and groups seen as anti-BJP. He also mentions 2.54 lakh appeals filed in West Bengal against voters whom judicial officers had already found eligible.

The CPI(ML) surveyed 50 booths in Bihar, and comparing the old and new lists, the rate of wrongly removed names came to 17 percent. The writer concludes that when even the Supreme Court has given the Commission a free hand, democracy now rests on the political sense of citizens, and the decision will be made on the streets.
nazar: This is an article by a party leader, so its figures and charges should be read with that in mind. But the question about Forms 6 and 7 is not a party question: if a citizen whose name was cut has to prove their identity all over again, the hardest blow will fall on those with the fewest papers, that is, workers, migrants, women and minorities. The Commission should make public the reason for every name it cut.
sawal: How fair is it to call a citizen whose name was cut a 'new voter'?
ref: Form 6 and Form 7
Form 6 is for adding a name to the voter list for the first time; Form 7 is for objecting to a name or getting it removed.
SIR
The Special Intensive Revision, a process of checking the voter list afresh by going door to door.

h: The 23 October protests and the government's dilemma
dek: According to Gyan Pathak, shutting Jantar Mantar did not stop the movement; instead it has begun to spread from lane to lane.
body: On 12 October, Jantar Mantar was removed from the list of protest sites. It was the only designated place near the seat of power. In its place the government suggested three sites, all far from the city. Gyan Pathak says this backfired, and instead of being confined to one spot, the movement is now scattering and spreading.

The second round began on 10 October with a call from the Cockroach Janta Party. In response, thousands of people were detained, roads around Jantar Mantar were blocked, trains were cancelled and the internet was shut down. On 13 October, three of the party's leaders and many others were arrested for waving the tricolour. MPs of the INDIA alliance were also detained on two days in a row. On 16 October, ahead of a flag campaign in Connaught Place's Central Park, the park was shut for two days and the party's founder Abhijeet Dipke was detained, yet by evening hundreds of people had reached it.

The 23 October call comes from 'People Against SIR', which includes citizens' groups, students, farmers and minority organisations. The slogan is: a tricolour in every hand, a Jantar Mantar in every lane. There are four demands: removing Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, cancelling the SIR, withdrawing the 2023 law, and electoral reform including paper ballots.

According to the writer, the charge that more than 13 crore names were cut in the SIR has raised a question about the very legitimacy of democracy. The government has to do three things at once: not be seen crushing peaceful protest, defend the Commissioner without looking like a partner in taking away votes, and face the constitutional debate over the appointment law. Pathak believes that calling the protesters enemies of the country will do damage in return. The way forward is to restore trust, and the Commission's steps over the past month have not worked so far.
nazar: Taking away a place does not erase the questions. When one square is shut, every neighbourhood becomes a square, and that is harder for the government. The real issue is the crores of people whose names are alleged to have gone missing from the list, and most of them are poor, migrants and people on the margins. For them, the vote is the greatest power they have.
sawal: Can trust in democracy be saved by taking away the place to protest?
ref: SIR
The Special Intensive Revision of the voter list. There are charges that the names of a large number of valid voters were cut in it.
The 2023 law
The law on appointing the Chief Election Commissioner and commissioners, which removed the Chief Justice from the selection committee.

h: Six questions for the Commission that remain unanswered
dek: Raising questions about the 2024 voter list, the 2023 law, ECINET and the court's 'clean chit', A J Prabal shows that the movement's demands are not empty.
body: Writing this article on Gandhi Jayanti, A J Prabal saw the start of a new freedom struggle on the street. More than seven hundred people were detained in Delhi and thousands gathered at Mumbai's Shivaji Park. In his view, the 'impeachment' of the Chief Election Commissioner has already begun on the street, and the demand for resignation is only the first step.

The first question is about the 2024 voter list. According to the writer, it was the last list that was not disputed across the country, and the court accepted it too. The SIR instead put the burden of proving eligibility on the citizen, even though changes to a list usually come gradually, not in sudden jumps.

The second question is about the 2023 law that gave the Prime Minister and a minister of his choice a majority in appointing commissioners, even though a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court had said the Chief Justice should be on the committee. The same law also gave the commissioners lifelong protection from criminal prosecution.

The third question is about technology. The writer explains that the old ERONET left the decision to the officer, while the new ECINET makes the Commission's IT department the final judge. Citing news reports, he charges that two commissioners objected to this in writing and asked for an audit, and that the Deputy Election Commissioner who pushed the audit forward was transferred.

Finally, he questions the Supreme Court's 'clean chit': the court held the Commission's power to be valid, but did not test the honesty with which that power was used. When trust in institutions is this low, says the writer, sustained protest and the legal fight must go on side by side.
nazar: This article takes the movement beyond slogans and turns it into a charter of demands. When an algorithm cuts names in the name of 'logical errors' and the blame is put on some BLO (booth-level officer), the first to be pushed out are those whose names are spelt differently on every paper: migrant workers, Adivasis (indigenous people), poor women.
The questions are right, but their answers will not come as a favour from any court or commission. They will have to be asked again and again, both on the street and in Parliament.
sawal: Should the final word on the voter list rest with an officer or with software?
ref: ECINET
The Election Commission's new centralised digital platform, which brings together more than forty applications. Critics say it has reduced the judgment of local officers.
The 2023 law
The law on appointing the Chief Election Commissioner and other commissioners, which removed the Chief Justice from the selection committee and put in a minister chosen by the Prime Minister.
photo_note: Purification by Muddy Water, a cartoon by Gaganendranath Tagore

h: 47 lakh names off Delhi's list, and Modi's dilemma
dek: Vir Sanghvi argues that even if the government shields Gyanesh Kumar and wins Uttar Pradesh, the credibility of that win will stay in question.
body: Vir Sanghvi recalls that when the Jantar Mantar movement began, nobody in the corridors of power took it seriously. Earlier protests against paper leaks had quickly fallen apart, and the Cockroach Janta Party was written off as social media noise. The government thought tough police action would send the young people, especially the young women, back home. According to the writer, the opposite happened: police brutality turned public opinion towards the protesters.

According to the writer, the government's plan was simple: reach young people in the language of selfie videos, and win Uttar Pradesh next year to show that Modi's standing is intact. In this plan, the Chief Election Commissioner only had to stay quiet. Sanghvi says that instead, he did something in Delhi that brought the BJP no benefit at all.

Out of Delhi's roughly 1.45 crore voters, about 47 lakh names were cut in the counting stage itself. Of the remaining 97 lakh, around 33 lakh got notices, and many of these were elderly people and BJP supporters. For now, the writer calls this incompetence, not rigging.

Then came the Form 6 matter. The charge is that this form for adding new voters was changed without authority, and the Commission said the court had approved it. Chief Justice Surya Kant said in open court that no such approval had been given. Sanghvi sees this as an unprecedented rebuke for the Commission.

According to him, Modi has two paths. If he keeps Kumar, people will believe the government needs a discredited officer to win elections, and even the UP win will not be spotless. If he removes him, the protesters will be emboldened, but winning without Kumar will give the government the moral high ground.
nazar: Sanghvi's sums are electoral, but his figures tell a bigger story on their own: one in every three voters in a city was questioned. In a country where the elderly and the poor have to hunt for papers to keep their own vote, the difference between 'incompetence' and 'rigging' means nothing to the voter whose name was cut.
The article also shows that a movement dismissed as social media noise upset the government's whole ready-made plan.
sawal: How much of a win is a win in an election under doubt?
ref: Form 6
The form for adding a new name to the voter list, whose format is laid down in the Registration of Electors Rules of 1960.
Sharp Edge
Vir Sanghvi's regular column in ThePrint.

h: Learn from Champaran, Aakar Patel tells the government
dek: According to Aakar Patel, even the British bowed to peaceful protest and corrected an injustice, and today's government should learn from that.
body: In this column written after Gandhi Jayanti, Aakar Patel reminds us that the right to gather peacefully and clean elections are both foundations of democracy. He charges that the government is stopping people from gathering today so that no one can demand answers from Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and that its attitude is roughly: do what you like.

Then he goes back to Champaran in 1917. There, under the tinkathia system, farmers were forced to grow indigo on part of their land. When the 47-year-old Gandhi arrived to investigate, the magistrate ordered him to leave the district. Gandhi refused to obey the order, but kept cooperating with the officials and stayed completely calm. The British government withdrew the case, Lieutenant Governor Edward Gait set up an inquiry committee, the committee sided with the farmers, and a law was passed that ended tinkathia.

According to Patel, this is the conduct one expects of any government. He reminds us that after public anger over exam irregularities, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan had to be removed. Now the government is protecting the Commissioner because, according to the writer, he is very important to the BJP because of the SIR and the way the opposition has been treated. In his view, the small changes made to the SIR in a hurry are a sign of panic, and they have not calmed people's anger.

Gyanesh Kumar's term runs until January 2029, but Patel doubts the government can keep him that long. The farmers' movement, the anti-NRC movement and the Pradhan case show that when people hold firm, the government has to step back. He has three demands: the right to peaceful assembly should be respected, the injustice done to crores of voters should be reversed, and those responsible should be punished.
nazar: The Champaran example stings because it is about a colonial government that was not even answerable to the people. If the elected government of free India seems to listen even less than that, the question is bound to be asked. The farmers of the indigo fields and the voters cut from the list today are both asking for the same thing: to be heard.
sawal: Can an elected government be less accountable than a colonial one?
ref: Tinkathia
A system forced on farmers in Champaran, under which three kathas out of every twenty had to be planted with indigo.
Champaran Satyagraha
Gandhi's first big satyagraha (non-violent resistance), in Champaran, Bihar, in 1917, after which indigo farmers got relief.

h: Israel's election: the face may change, the thinking about war will not
dek: Paul Rogers argues that whether Netanyahu or Gadi Eisenkot wins Israel's election, military thinking treats permanent war as security.
body: Paul Rogers, professor emeritus of peace studies at the University of Bradford, looks at Israel's coming election with a bitter conclusion: whoever wins, the wars will not end. Since 7 October 2023, Israeli politics has shifted further to the right. Polls show that about three-quarters of people want to keep the army in Gaza and nearly 80 percent favour continuing the fight in Lebanon, while secular and liberal young people are leaving the country.

What is interesting is that in the latest polls the lead belongs not to Netanyahu but to the alliance of retired general Gadi Eisenkot. Eisenkot sat in the war cabinet after 7 October and left eight months later, saying the cabinet had failed in every one of its goals. Yet the same Eisenkot has been an advocate of the 'Dahiya doctrine', that is, large-scale bombing of civilian areas seen as the base of armed struggle. According to Rogers, the destruction of Gaza rested on this very thinking.

The article turns on a 2026 paper from Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, written by former military intelligence chief Tamir Hayman. Hayman says it is not his personal opinion but an assessment of top military thinking. It has five principles: Jewish identity above democracy, peace only as a temporary tool, Arab countries better kept weak, America as a declining power so war alone means security, and Palestinian nationalism as merely a Western story.

Rogers cuts these foundations down with facts. Between 2008 and 2021, more than five thousand Palestinians were killed in four 'deterrent' wars on Gaza, yet Israel did not become safe. Even after more than three years of fighting, the army has not been able to occupy the rest of Gaza.
He sees hope for change in soldiers' unease, allies drifting away and international pressure, but for now, in his view, Israel is shut inside a fortress of its own insecurity.
nazar: This article reminds us that elections change nothing until the basic thinking of power changes. If the face of the opposition is also a general's and its policy also one of bombing, then for Palestinians the vote only decides what the killer's name will be.

In India too, the habit of silencing every question in the name of 'security' has grown. In a society that takes war itself to be nationalism, minorities and people on the margins are the first to fall under suspicion.
sawal: Can a democracy remain a democracy alongside permanent war?
ref: Dahiya doctrine
A military doctrine that grew out of the destruction of Beirut's Dahiya district in the 2006 Lebanon war. It calls for using heavy force on civilian areas that support the enemy.
Gadi Eisenkot
Former chief of the Israeli army, who joined the war cabinet after 7 October and later split from Netanyahu to become a leading face of the opposition.

h: Brazil decides: Lula's return or the mafia's crowning
dek: Ahead of Sunday's second round, Benjamin Fogel says Flávio Bolsonaro's lead is shrinking and Lula is back in the race.
body: Brazil holds the second round of its presidential election on Sunday, and Jacobin's Benjamin Fogel feels that a contest that looked settled a few weeks ago has now opened up. In the first round, Flávio, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, was two points ahead, but in the latest Quaest poll his lead is just one point, 45 to 44. After a weak TV debate, the number of people who dislike him has also grown.

Fogel credits Lula's comeback to grassroots mobilisation: rallies on the streets and the digital campaign of MP André Janones, in which more than 8.2 million people have joined a WhatsApp channel called 'Lula's Army'. Then there is the law that came into force on 16 October for five days of work and two days off a week, which he sees as a major achievement of the Lula government.

A large part of the article is about the charges against Flávio. According to a magazine report, during the Covid period he was at a boat party with a man lobbying for vaccines, who allegedly gave him a Rolex watch. The writer charges that lawyers close to him were involved in laundering billions through online betting companies, that several of his associates were arrested in police operations, and that he has had ties with Rio's militias and a hired killer. Questions have also been raised about the rulings of the head of the electoral court.

Fogel calls this a 'post-civil-society election', where short videos on TikTok and Instagram shape opinion more than newspapers, and the scattered world of app-dependent workers becomes fertile ground for the right. Bolsonarism is now a digital mass party with about a quarter of the votes. Still, the writer concludes that the momentum is with Lula, and that his victory is essential for Brazil's sovereignty.
nazar: Brazil's fight feels familiar to us: politics run on WhatsApp, the nexus of crime and power, and questions raised about the courts. The difference is that there the left turned a concrete pro-worker promise, such as cutting working hours, into an electoral weapon.
The lesson for India's opposition is that the digital machine of hate is answered not by moral appeals alone, but by concrete work on livelihoods and organisation on the ground.
sawal: Can concrete pro-worker promises defeat digital hate?
ref: Bolsonarism
The far-right movement built around former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro. It includes praise for the military past, evangelical religiosity and propaganda that relies on social media.
8 January 2023
A week after Lula was sworn in, Bolsonaro supporters stormed Parliament, the Supreme Court and the presidential palace in Brasília.

h: More PF accounts, but not more secure jobs
dek: According to Santosh Mehrotra and Kingshuk Sarkar, the government's claim of a jobs boom based on EPFO data is misleading.
body: The government says jobs in the organised sector are growing fast, and offers the figures of the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation, or EPFO, as proof. Economists Santosh Mehrotra and Kingshuk Sarkar peel back the layers of this claim. They say that new names joining the PF (provident fund) do not mean new jobs. The count includes people changing jobs, people who were already working but have now come under PF, members rejoining, and paperwork changes. These figures were never designed to measure employment.

The real picture shows up in the sectors that could give work to people leaving farming. In 12 labour-intensive sectors such as textiles, leather, tea and diamond cutting, PF contributors fell by 1.3 percent between 2023-24 and 2025-26.

Citing the Annual Survey of Industries, the government says 57 lakh jobs were added in organised manufacturing. The writers point out that this count also includes owners, family members and unpaid workers. On top of that, the share of contract labour rose from 13 percent in 1993-94 to 40.7 percent in 2022-23, and contract workers usually get no social security.

The figure that stings most is that 90 percent of workers were informal in 2004-05, and 90 percent still are in 2024. The share of people in farming has risen instead of falling. By the writers' estimate, real wages have been stuck for 12 years, youth unemployment has doubled to 12 percent, and young people neither studying nor working have grown from five crore to ten crore. Their conclusion is that the test is not a name in a database, but lasting work at a decent wage.
nazar: The jobs debate has been trapped in a juggling act with numbers. When nine out of ten workers have no protection at all, a few lakh new PF accounts should be a reason not to celebrate but to look in the mirror.

The hardest blow falls on Dalit, Adivasi (indigenous), backward-caste and Muslim young people, who make up the largest share of contract and daily-wage work. Ten crore discouraged young people are a warning for any country, and the government should listen to it.
sawal: Ten crore young people are neither studying nor earning. Who is responsible?
ref: EPFO
The Employees' Provident Fund Organisation, which manages the PF and pensions of organised-sector employees. Its monthly figures are often presented as a measure of jobs.
PLFS
The Periodic Labour Force Survey, the government's regular survey that gives figures on employment, unemployment and the kind of work people do.

h: In Bihar, asking for wages can still cost a life
dek: Through two incidents in Nalanda and Rohtas, Ashok Kumar Chandravanshi asks when the weak worker in the village will be able to demand his due without fear.
body: Ashok Kumar Chandravanshi, a senior advocate at the Patna High Court, sees two incidents in Bihar not as separate crimes but as symptoms of one disease. The first took place in Darua Beldari village in the Noorsarai police station area of Nalanda. On 4 October, Kamo Chauhan, about 30 years old, helped cook at a brahmbhoj (a feast held after a death). When the work was done he asked for his wages, and a dispute broke out. His family charges that he was beaten and pushed into a pan of boiling oil. After being taken through several hospitals, he died in Patna on 12 October.

According to the writer, the police carried out raids and named two people as the main accused, but there is also a charge that the village headman tried to arrange a settlement for Rs 2.65 lakh and, with a promise of treatment, get the injured man himself to admit fault. These charges are still under investigation.

The second incident is from Jogia village in the Dinara police station area of Rohtas, where Chandeshwar Chaudhary, about 60 years old, was shot dead on 5 August. News reports spoke of a grudge over wages, old dues and his working for someone else. His body was later found in a canal in Buxar, there was violence and arson in the village, and the investigation was handed to the CID.

Chandravanshi's argument is simple: every worker has the right to ask for better wages and to change employers, and no one can be forced to work for a particular household. He cites Articles 14, 21, 23 and 39 of the Constitution and says that wherever caste oppression appears, the relevance of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act should be examined. He also warns against passing judgment on all of Bihar or on any caste from two incidents, but says social justice is not only a share in power; it is also the fearless voice of the weakest worker.
nazar: These incidents show that in the village, wages are still seen not as a deal but as a favour, and the punishment for questioning that favour is sometimes a life. Hushing up a case with money in the name of a settlement is a new form of the same old power.

In Bihar, the politics of social justice changed the face of power, but the system that protects people who work in fields, kitchens and brick kilns is still weak. Enforcing the minimum wage and quick, fair investigations are the first conditions for changing that.
sawal: Who in the village stands up to stop violence over a demand for wages?
ref: Article 23
The provision of the Constitution that bans begar (unpaid forced labour) and every kind of forced labour.
Prevention of Atrocities Act
The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act of 1989, which provides strict punishment and special courts for caste crimes against these communities.

h: The death of the welfare state and the road after it
dek: Aasim Sajjad Akhtar says the student movement in France has proved that the welfare state is finished and will not come back on its own.
body: Aasim Sajjad Akhtar, who teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, sees the current movement in France as the seal on the end of an era. In his view, the upheaval there, which began with students' anger over run-down schools, shows that the welfare state is now formally dead, and that this is true not only of education but of the whole developed world.

After the Second World War, most people in Western Europe, North America and Australia were guaranteed public education, healthcare, water, electricity and unemployment benefits. Akhtar stresses that this was not a gift from the rulers. They were afraid of their own working class and of the colonies in Asia and Africa that might turn towards Soviet or Chinese socialism. Capital accepted controlled profits and high taxes, and workers gave up the road of revolution.

This bargain began to crack with neoliberalism in the late 1970s and broke with the end of the Cold War. The institutions and people's hopes survived, so the death was slow, but stagnant incomes and growing inequality gave ground to right-wing hate. Britain's Labour Party and France's Socialist Party abandoned the left path, and America now wants neither to support Europe nor to help poor countries.

The writer also reminds us that the golden age of welfare in rich countries was an age of coups, wars and aid dependence in the Third World, from Ayub Khan's Pakistan to Vietnam, Congo and Chile. In Pakistan the welfare era never came at all; the state kept its colonial temper, and today its only concerns are profit and repression. His conclusion is that the old model will not return, and that a new prosperity needs both ideology and organisation.
nazar: Akhtar's argument applies just as well to India. Here, welfare has been turned from a right into a gift for the 'labharthi' (beneficiary), with free rations, while secure jobs and good public schools and hospitals keep falling behind.

The lesson of history is that rights were never handed down as charity from above; they were won through organised pressure from below. For communities on the margins, the real question is how that pressure can be built again.
sawal: Can beneficiary schemes take the place of the welfare state?
ref: Welfare state
A system in which the government takes responsibility for basic needs such as education, health, pensions and unemployment benefits. This model spread in Europe after the Second World War.
Marshall Plan
America's programme of economic aid to rebuild Western Europe after the Second World War, which is also linked to Cold War strategy.

h: Sri Lanka: a monk's robe is not above the law
dek: On the demand to free Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara, Asoka Seneviratne says that changing court rulings under pressure from religious crowds will hollow out equal citizenship.
body: In Sri Lanka, sections of the Buddhist Sangha (monastic order) are on the streets over the imprisonment of hardline Buddhist monk Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara Thero and the demand for his release. Professor Asoka S. Seneviratne does not see this as a matter of one monk or one sentence. For him, the real question is how a democratic society balances respect for religion, a monk's discipline, the rule of law and the authority of an elected government.

Behind the case is a sentence for contempt of court. A presidential pardon he had received earlier was cancelled, and the rest of the sentence came into force. Some monks have also objected to the prison uniform. The writer sees this as a separate legal question, and says any change to prison rules should be transparent and equal for all, not a concession given under political pressure.

According to Seneviratne, democracy is not just elections but a way of living, which includes equality before the law, independent institutions and peaceful dissent. Monks and citizens can criticise policies and protest within the law. He reminds us that in history monks advised kings, but giving advice does not give the right to give orders. Renunciation is made not by a robe or rank, but by inner moral discipline.

The court had to step in over the protests near the Presidential Secretariat in Colombo. The writer warns that using religious feeling to pressure courts and officials turns legal questions into a show of strength, and decisions start being made not on the merits of a case but by the size of the crowd. A country recovering from an economic crisis needs institutions it can trust. His conclusion is that the government should listen to religious concerns but not give up its constitutional duty.
nazar: Gnanasara has been a leader of the Bodu Bala Sena and has faced serious charges of stirring up hatred against Muslims. A religious crowd demanding a concession above the law for such a man is the story of all of South Asia, where those who speak against minorities in the name of the majority's faith often get a free pass.

In India too, action against inflammatory speeches by leaders in saffron robes often goes soft. Sri Lanka's test is a mirror for us as well: is the law equal for everyone, or does it bend when it sees a crowd?
sawal: Should courts bow before religious crowds?
ref: Bodu Bala Sena
A Sinhala Buddhist nationalist group in Sri Lanka, linked to charges of stirring up anti-Muslim violence, including the 2014 Aluthgama riots.
Bhikkhu
The Pali word for a Buddhist monk; bhikshu in Sanskrit. It refers to a person who has taken up a life of renunciation and moral discipline.

h: JNU PhD seats: 56 of 84 programmes have not a single Adivasi seat
dek: BAPSA's count says that this year ST students got a 5.3 percent share of 711 seats instead of 7.5, and the Dalit quota was not filled even once in seven rounds.
body: In a statement on 19 October, the Birsa Ambedkar Phule Students' Association (BAPSA) charged that Jawaharlal Nehru University has broken its own reservation standard in PhD admissions for 2026-27. The prospectus says 7.5 percent for Scheduled Tribes, but only 38 of the 711 seats are for ST candidates, that is, 5.3 percent. By the group's count there should have been 53 seats, about 15 fewer than due.

The problem lies in the distribution. Of the 84 programmes that announced admissions, 56 have not a single ST seat, while 24 of these do have EWS (economically weaker sections) seats. In 30 programmes, no ST seat has come up for four rounds in a row. Biotechnology, Computational Sciences and the School of Sanskrit and Indic Studies have zero ST seats this time. In the data for seven rounds, the 15 percent SC share was not filled even once, while the quotas for other categories were filled or overfilled.

BAPSA also questions the interview, which carries 30 percent weight. It cites the 2012 Rajeev Bhatt committee, which found that SC/ST candidates got 19 to 20 percent lower marks in the viva, and the 2016 Nafey committee's recommendation to cut this weight to 15 percent. The demands are that a corrigendum be issued to add 15 ST seats, that reservation be audited by programme and centre, and that JNU's own entrance exam be brought back. The report carries no response from the university.
nazar: Showing the quota as filled in the total while making it vanish programme by programme is the office-desk way of exclusion. When the doors of subjects like science and Sanskrit have been shut to Adivasi (indigenous) researchers for years, the question is not only about seats but about whose hands knowledge stays in. The university should make its roster public; that is its duty, not a favour.
sawal: Why is there no place for Adivasi researchers in fifty-six programmes?
ref: Roster
The list used to apply reservation, which decides which seat goes to which category. If it is not clear in small programmes, the quota stays only on paper.
BAPSA
The Birsa Ambedkar Phule Students' Association, an Ambedkarite student group at JNU, formed in 2014.
photo_note: Representative image: a building at Aligarh Muslim University

h: The election commissioners' letters and the Cabinet Secretary's silence
dek: Papers obtained under RTI show that two election commissioners sought action against a senior officer, and the Cabinet Secretariat put off a decision, calling action 'inappropriate'.
body: Transparency campaigner Commodore Lokesh Batra has obtained some documents under the Right to Information that show the tug of war inside the Election Commission. Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi wrote letters to Cabinet Secretary T V Somanathan seeking action against Senior Deputy Election Commissioner Maneesh Garg.

The charge was that within just a few hours of getting additional charge of administration, Garg redistributed work among officers, including officers senior to him, even though both commissioners had said again and again that this should not be done without the Commission's approval. According to an Indian Express investigation in September, this reshuffle removed the IAS officer who was overseeing the Commission's IT department. Both commissioners said that under the 2023 law, such decisions are made by the three commissioners together or by majority, and on 30 July they even reversed that order.

The Cabinet Secretariat's file records that the commissioners sent these letters in their personal capacity, not on behalf of the whole Commission, so action without the formal view of all three commissioners could be seen as interference in a constitutional body. The Secretariat only sent an acknowledgement and spoke of seeking the view of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The report does not say any action was taken against Garg, and it carries no response from any side.
nazar: At a time when questions are being raised across the country about the voter list and the IT system, the objection of two commissioners to the removal of oversight over that very IT department is no small matter. If even two of the Commission's three members cannot take their point forward, then whose independence does 'independent institution' really mean?
sawal: Who removed oversight of the Commission's IT department, and why?
ref: RTI
The Right to Information Act, 2005. Through it, any citizen can ask government offices for records.
The 2023 Election Commissioners law
The law on the appointment and working of the Chief Election Commissioner and commissioners. It says the Commission's decisions are to be taken unanimously or by majority.

h: Neha Bora's 'Bangladesh model': a whole charge built from half a video
dek: An Alt News check: a message of solidarity sent to a student conference was cut and trimmed and passed off as a call for violence.
body: At a press conference in Delhi on 15 October, BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari said AISA president Neha Bora wants to repeat a Bangladesh-style Gen Z uprising in India. IANS posted the statement, the BJP's official handle put out a video with a short clip of Bora's speech attached, many right-wing accounts called it a demand for a 'violent coup' against the government, and Arnab Goswami repeated the same on TV.

Alt News watched the full video. It was a message of about one and three-quarter minutes that Bora sent on 13 October to the sixth central conference of the Socialist Students' Front, a left student group in Bangladesh, because problems with her passport and visa kept her from going herself. In the message she spoke of drawing inspiration from the student movement there and listed the shared struggles of both countries: votes and democratic rights, religious extremism, and the privatisation of education. At the end she expressed the hope of working together for a better South Asia.

The viral clip left out the context of the conference and the parts about democratic rights. The secretary of the Socialist Party of Bangladesh (Marxist) also said the words had been taken out of context. Bora claims that even the conference logo was removed from the footage. Alt News has called the claim misleading: there is no call for violence in India in it.
nazar: Linking young people in movements to a 'foreign conspiracy' is an old weapon, and this time it was fired from the ruling party's official account. When even a message of solidarity is served up as sedition, the question is who will hold those who spread such lies to account.
sawal: When will there be action against the official account that ran half a video?
ref: Taking out of context
Presenting a piece of a statement apart from its occasion and the rest of what was said, so that the meaning changes. In fact-check language this is a 'misleading' claim.
AISA
The All India Students' Association, a left student group linked to the CPI(ML) Liberation.

h: Criticising the Babri verdict is no crime: Karnataka High Court quashes case
dek: The court ended a case against 13 people over posters put up in Mangaluru in 2019, holding it to be the right to dissent.
body: In an order of 15 October, Justice H P Sandesh of the Karnataka High Court quashed a criminal case that had been running since 2019 against 13 people in Mangaluru. They were accused of putting up posters calling the Supreme Court's Babri Masjid verdict a 'denial of justice'.

In November 2019, a five-judge Constitution Bench had ruled that the entire disputed land be given to the Ram temple trust. A few days later, on 16 November, Mangaluru South police took suo motu (on their own) notice and filed a case against Muhammad Hanif and others under Sections 153A and 295A of the IPC. The prosecution said the posters spread ill will between communities.

The petitioners' lawyer cited the Supreme Court's 2024 Javed Ahmad Hajam ruling, which said that dissent from government decisions is protected under Articles 19 and 21. The High Court held that the posters only expressed disagreement with the verdict and raised a voice for justice, and that the aim was not to spread hatred. The court also said that resentment arising in some people's minds is not enough to apply 153A.
nazar: The ruling is right, but it took seven years. For all those years, 13 people kept making rounds of the courts because they had disagreed with the highest court. This process is the real punishment, and sections like 153A often do this very job against Muslims and dissenting voices. The police who file false cases should also be made to answer.
sawal: Who will account for these seven years of trouble?
ref: Section 153A
A section of the old IPC that made it a crime to stir up enmity between groups on grounds of religion, caste or language. It has now been replaced by a new section in the BNS.
Javed Ahmad Hajam ruling
In 2024, quashing a case against a professor who had criticised the removal of Article 370, the Supreme Court said every citizen has the right to criticise the government.

h: The tyre poison that no one in India is even measuring
dek: 6PPD-quinone, formed from wearing tyres, has been linked to mass fish deaths in America, but there is no data on it in India's roads and drains.
body: All over the world, a chemical called 6PPD is added to tyres to make them last longer. As tyres wear down, it reacts with ozone in the air to form 6PPD-quinone, which scientists count among the most toxic compounds for aquatic life. In the rain, it washes off roads into rivers and lakes.

In 2020, a study in the journal Science solved the mystery of the deaths of coho salmon returning to urban streams in America. After rain, about 90 percent of the fish would die. Causes such as temperature, disease, oxygen and pesticides were ruled out one by one, and in the end this very tyre chemical turned out to be responsible.

India is now the world's third largest vehicle market. Vehicle sales grew 10.4 percent in 2025-26 and tyre production also keeps rising. Yet according to N Jayaraman, a chemist at IISc Bengaluru, there is not a single scientific data point on this chemical in the country's road dust, stormwater or water bodies. Most cities have no separate system for rainwater, drains carry untreated sewage, and heavy rain can increase the danger. Crumb from old tyres is also filled into artificial turf fields. Jayaraman calls for a policy on this right away.
nazar: What is not measured does not show up as harm in government papers either. Fishers who live off rivers and the poor who live along their banks will pay the first price. Pollution boards should add tyre chemicals to their testing lists before dead fish become the data themselves.
sawal: How much tyre poison is in our drains and rivers?
ref: 6PPD-quinone
A compound formed when the tyre chemical 6PPD meets ozone. Even in very small amounts it is deadly for fish.
Stormwater
Rainwater that runs off roads and roofs into drains, carrying the dirt, oil and chemicals along the way with it.

h: Heatwave or flood, the gig worker has no right to say no
dek: Apps decide when and how much work there will be, and the new labour codes have no firm rule on working hours or protection from heat for these workers.
body: Ganga (name changed), 43, from Faridabad, works as a beautician for Urban Company. During heavy rain in May 2026 she tried to cancel a booking, and the app refused. Cancelling more than four bookings in 28 days leads to retraining or temporary suspension, and now, instead of letting her choose bookings, the app hands them out itself. The company asks for at least six hours a day and at least fourteen hours over the weekends of a month.

In a Janpahal survey of a thousand platform workers in ten cities, 57 percent were found to work more than 49 hours a week, and 23 percent more than 70 hours. Three-quarters reported bad effects from heat. According to HeatWatch's 2026 report on women gig workers, 71 percent work all seven days in summer, and 74 percent got no help from any platform during heatwaves.

The 2020 OSH Code sets a limit of eight hours a day, but gig workers do not come under it. The Social Security Code leaves the making of schemes to the government's will. The NDMA's 2025 advisory, that work should not be required between 11 am and 4 pm during heatwave alerts, is not binding. In June 2026, India did not vote on the ILO convention on platform work. The companies and the Labour Ministry did not answer questions.
nazar: By calling the gig worker a 'partner', the companies have freed themselves of every responsibility of an employer, while it is the app that gives the orders. In a time of climate crisis, the right to refuse work and a place to rest in the heat should be basic labour rights, not charity. Laws in states like Karnataka and Bihar show the way, and the Centre should not lag behind.
sawal: When the app is the boss, how is the worker a 'partner'?
ref: OSH Code
The 2020 labour law on occupational safety, health and working conditions, which merged several older laws.
NDMA
The National Disaster Management Authority, which issues guidelines on disasters such as heatwaves and floods.

h: Araku coffee: a costly cup, and women left off the land papers
dek: In the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh, Adivasi women grow and dry the famous Araku coffee, but the land is not in their names and they have no say over the price.
body: In the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh, about a thousand metres above sea level, the village of Karakaputtu lies in the Paderu Agency area, home to Scheduled Tribe communities. Here the Konda Dora women, such as Surra Pushpa and her companions, take turns working on each other's fields without wages. Paddy in the rains, and turmeric, millets, black pepper and coffee in the other seasons: some crop or other passes through their hands all year. These same women grow the GI-tagged Araku Arabica, which sells in the market for anywhere from one thousand to fourteen thousand rupees a kilo.

Coffee came to the area in British times, and after 1970 the Coffee Board and the Integrated Tribal Development Agency (ITDA) spread it. First, silver oak saplings are planted for shade, then coffee beneath them, and it can take up to eight years for the plants to bear fruit. Clearing the fields, weeding, picking the ripe cherries in the bitter cold from November to January, then drying them in the sun for weeks and guarding them, this is mostly women's work. The men handle the pulping machines and the fire lines.

Despite this, in the government's books these women are not farmers, because a farmer's identity is tied to ownership of land, and land usually goes to sons. Pushpa's mother-in-law, Surra Parvatamma, farmed about ten acres with her husband for fifty years, but six years after his death the land is still not in her name; officials say a survey must come first. The ITDA does not keep separate figures for women and men, while the Girijan Cooperative Corporation estimates that about 40 percent of coffee farmers are women. Money from PM-KISAN and the state scheme also goes to the name of the landowner.

The arithmetic of earnings is even more crooked. The government corporation buys less than five percent of the area's produce; the rest is picked up by moneylenders from the cities of the plains, who pay 10 to 50 percent less than the government price but also lend money without papers. According to the report, switching moneylenders means losing future credit, so the farmers stay tied. Women of the Kondu, a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group, got only 250 rupees a kilo for parchment coffee, while the same coffee later sells for over two thousand rupees a kilo under the name 'coffee by Adivasi women'.

On top of this comes the weather: this year the rain was well below normal, and dangerously hot days are increasing. In the report, people from farmers' groups point out that the National Policy for Farmers 2007 keeps a broad definition of a farmer, and that the Women Farmers' Entitlements Bill of 2013 lapsed without being passed. Pushpa's answer is simple: she is a farmer.
nazar: The Araku story shows that the profit from a brand and a GI tag reaches the top, not the bottom. Until land titles, joint forest rights and government purchase reach women's names, their labour will keep selling under someone else's label.

In Fifth Schedule areas there is a law to stop land from passing into outside hands, but the same intrusion is coming in through the back door of the market and debt. Increasing government purchase and setting prices in line with the market would be the first step.
sawal: Why does a woman who farms the land need a title to count as a farmer?
ref: GI tag
Geographical Indication: the legal identity given to a special product of a particular region, such as Darjeeling tea or Araku coffee.
Fifth Schedule
The part of the Constitution that makes special arrangements for the administration of Adivasi-majority areas and the protection of their land.
Parchment coffee
Coffee beans washed and dried after pulping, on which a thin layer still remains.

h: Arundhati Roy at Jantar Mantar: laughter brought down the wall of an image
dek: In a conversation with Scroll, Arundhati Roy describes how young people's memes and jokes undid in two weeks an image built over twenty-four years.
by: Arundhati Roy, in conversation with Supriya Sharma
body: This is a short video conversation from Scroll, recorded at Jantar Mantar in Delhi. Scroll's executive editor Supriya Sharma asks the questions and the writer Arundhati Roy answers them. The conversation is from the Monday when the young people's sit-in ended, a day after Prime Minister Narendra Modi had removed his education minister to cool the anger of the youth a little.

The background is that in May, the paper of an exam was leaked. Students and unemployed young people took to the streets against this. According to Scroll, the movement flared up further when the Delhi Police lathi-charged (attacked with batons) the protesters and fired pellets. In answer to the batons, the young people did what was in their hands: a flood of jokes, memes and posts mocking the Prime Minister.

This movement calls itself the Cockroach. It began with a parody account on social media, after unemployed young people and activists were called cockroaches in a judge's remark. The young people made that very insult their name. Roy says this movement has already achieved far more than it set out to.

The most important part of the conversation is about the politics of laughter. Roy believes a joke squeezes politics down and puts its essence in front of us. What does not get across through long speeches and articles reaches millions of people through one sharp meme. She openly praises the boldness and the cheek of these memes.

Roy's main argument is about Modi's image. According to her, this image was carefully built since 2002, that is, for about twenty-four years, and in all this time the Prime Minister never faced an open press conference. Young people stripped away this image, built by avoiding questions, in just two weeks.

From this comes the question at the centre of the conversation: does the Prime Minister even know what the country's young people are saying about him, or does the circle around him keep him shielded from these voices?

Scroll has titled the conversation after Roy's remark that the young people getting the better of the Prime Minister is a bigger thing than winning an election. The video is short, but it gathers in one place the restlessness of those months when the country's youth were on the street with questions of exams, jobs and dignity.
nazar: This video reminds us that questions like unemployment and paper leaks are not only failures of administration, but a matter of the future of crores of young people. When institutions do not answer, laughter becomes the language of protest, and power is often most rattled by this very laughter.
The real test will be whether this anger can move beyond memes into concrete demands for jobs, a transparent exam system and the right to peaceful protest.
sawal: Can jokes and memes win accountability from power?
ref: Jantar Mantar
The place near Parliament in Delhi that has for decades been the spot for sit-ins and protests.
Paper leak
When a question paper gets out before an exam, washing away the hard work of lakhs of candidates.
Pellets
Shotgun pellets, whose use on crowds human rights groups have long questioned.

h: Anne Carson: poetry that speaks in the empty spaces
dek: Writing for Sammukh, poet Shivprasad Joshi moves through the books of this year's Nobel winner Anne Carson and shows how fragments, silence and politics travel together in her work.
body: After the Canadian writer Anne Carson won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature, Sammukh asked the poet Shivprasad Joshi to write about her. According to Joshi, Carson is the nineteenth woman to receive the honour and the second from Canada after Alice Munro. He says he first met Carson in the pages of the British magazine Granta.

Joshi sees Carson as a writer who dwells on small, unnoticed things and builds her structures from fragments of Greek myths, Sappho, Euripides and Aristotle. In her work the borders between essay, poem and collage melt away. The empty space left on the page, the smudges and the broken lines say as much as the words.

The article moves through several books. Joshi calls 'Wrong Norma' a museum of fragments, which has a long essay against drone strikes and bombing, and also a poem on the case of the Yemeni engineer Faisal bin Ali Jaber in an American court. 'Nox' is an elegy for her brother's death, where grief is recorded in blank pages. In 'Autobiography of Red', the old myth of Geryon and Herakles becomes the story of two lovers instead of hunted and hunter.
Joshi also mentions 'The Beauty of the Husband' and 'The Glass Essay', which carry the pain of breaking relationships, and draws an interesting comparison with Orhan Pamuk's 'My Name Is Red'.
His conclusion is that Carson does not fit in any one box, and that her writing asks the reader to feel within themselves the suffering of people far away, including the children killed in Gaza.
nazar: In Hindi, writing on foreign Nobel winners is often only news-like comment. Joshi's article goes further and shows that experimental poetry does not turn away from questions of war and power either.
This poetry, which speaks of ordinary people caught between drones, prisons and courts, reminds the Hindi reader that experiments with form and political conscience are not enemies of each other.
sawal: Can the silence of poetry also be a language of protest?
ref: Sappho
A poet of ancient Greece whose poems survive mostly in fragments. Carson has also translated her.
Collage
A work made by joining different pieces together, whether in pictures or in writing.
photo_note: A fresco from Pompeii, linked to Sappho

h: Padma Sachdev's Dogri story: the closed door of a daughter's old home
dek: On Sammukh, Yogita Yadav has begun a new series of translated Dogri stories, and the first is a story by Padma Sachdev in which the marriage of two little girls becomes the punishment of their lives.
body: A story by Padma Sachdev, who is regarded as the first modern woman poet of Dogri, has now come out in Hindi. The fiction writer Yogita Yadav has begun a new series on Sammukh in which the translation of a Dogri story will appear on the 22nd of every month. This story is the first in the series.

The story is set in the Duggar region. Two daughters of a family in Jammu, one nine years old and the other eleven, are married into the same household so that the two can support each other in a strange land. Along with the dowry goods, they travel by tonga (horse cart) and then palanquin towards Ramnagar, spending the night at an inn on the way. The sisters' small squabbles, the younger one secretly eating sweets, the elder one acting grown-up, all this gives the story the colour of childhood, but beneath it runs a bitter truth: in those days it was almost impossible for a daughter to return to her parents' home after marriage.

The story then moves some fifteen years ahead. At the farewell of a daughter of the royal family, she is invited to visit her parents' home, and word spreads that perhaps that road will now open for daughters. In this hope, the two sisters' brothers secretly reach Ramnagar to meet them. But the sisters know that without the king's permission this meeting could bring trouble for their brothers, and the story ends at a painful turn.

At the end of the presentation there is also an introduction to the life and works of Padma Sachdev (1940-2021). She had received the Padma Shri and the Sahitya Akademi award. The translator, Yogita Yadav, is herself a well-known fiction writer.
nazar: Stories in languages like Dogri often stay far from the Hindi reader, though they record a history of the women of the hills that is not found in the chronicles of royal courts. This pain of child marriage, dowry and being cut off from one's parents' home is not the tale of one princely state; it is the story of a whole system in which a woman's wishes were decided by someone else's order. A Dogri story coming into Hindi every month is important work in building bridges between smaller languages.
sawal: Does a daughter's parental home still depend on someone else's permission?
ref: Duggar
The Dogri-speaking region of Jammu and its surroundings. The names of the Dogra dynasty and the Dogri language come from it.
Padma Sachdev
A writer in Dogri and Hindi (1940-2021), regarded as the first modern woman poet of Dogri.
photo_note: Rama and Lakshmana on a mountain, Shangri Ramayana

h: 'Court Martial': it shows the Dalit's pain, not his voice
dek: On Hindwi Bela, Kanu Priya rereads Swadesh Deepak's famous play and asks why its Dalit hero does not speak.
body: Kanu Priya begins at a dinner table. An elderly relative asks her caste outright, and before she can say anything, a friend of her mother's answers for her that she does not believe in caste. The writer values the good intention, but she feels that the right to give her own answer was taken from her. This experience leads her to Swadesh Deepak's 'Court Martial'.

The play has been staged many times. There was Ranjit Kapoor's direction, more than four hundred and fifty shows by Arvind Gaur's Asmita Theatre, Mahmood Farooqui's 2016 production with prisoners in Tihar Jail, and a 2020 film adaptation. The story is of Ramchander, a Dalit soldier, who is tried for killing his officer after constant caste humiliation.

The writer's objections work on several levels. Ramchander mostly sits silent with his head bowed, which makes him look guilty and crushed. The oppressive officer is made such a personal villain that caste starts to look like the problem of one bad man instead of a structure. Ramchander breaking down in tears during his testimony reminds her of Chinua Achebe's criticism of Conrad for taking away the voice of Africans.

The ending troubles her too. The judge privately praises Ramchander but hands down a death sentence, and then the oppressive officer's suicide is called 'poetic justice'. According to the writer, the message that comes out of this is that there is no hope of changing the structure.

Her conclusion is that the play brings Dalit suffering to the stage, but not Dalit consciousness. Its feeling is one of sympathy, not of claiming rights, and despite all his sensitivity, the writer stays within the frame of the upper-caste point of view.
nazar: This article puts forward the uncomfortable question that progressive Hindi theatre often avoids: showing someone's pain and letting them speak for themselves are two different things.
The story at the start takes this debate out of the book and into the drawing room, where even well-meaning people start speaking on others' behalf.
sawal: When does sympathy start taking away someone's voice?
ref: Poetic justice
An ending in a story or play where the bad are punished and the good rewarded, often with the help of coincidence.
Chinua Achebe
The Nigerian novelist who called Joseph Conrad's 'Heart of Darkness' racist for showing Africans as voiceless.

h: Two novels by Elif Shafak and the silences of history
dek: In Hindwi Bela's series 'Jagah-Jagah 2.0' (Here and There), Nishant Kaushik reads two of Shafak's less discussed novels, on the Turkish-Armenian wound and Ottoman architecture.
body: Nishant Kaushik reminds us that the big concerns of twentieth-century Turkish fiction have been the tension between modernity and Islam, Turkish, Armenian and Kurdish identities, and the memory of the Ottoman Empire. Elif Shafak, who lives in London and writes in English, touches these delicate subjects with courage. Kaushik admits that his old opinion of her, formed after reading 'The Forty Rules of Love', was hasty.

The first novel is 'The Bastard of Istanbul' (2006), which looks at the Turkish-Armenian relationship, made bitter by the massacres and deportations of 1915, through two families. Through Asya, nineteen, raised among women in Istanbul, and Armanoush, an Armenian-American who has come to search for her roots, the novel asks how societies remember, forget and suppress history. According to the writer, even forgotten history stays alive in food, names and family stories. Its weakness is that the novel sprawls more than it needs to.

The second novel, 'The Architect's Apprentice', goes back to the sixteenth century, where Jahan, apprentice to the great architect Mimar Sinan, and a white elephant named Chota are at the centre of the story. The tale travels from the court of Istanbul to Rome and Agra, and real figures such as Sultan Suleiman, Sinan and Michelangelo move alongside invented characters.

Kaushik shows that Shafak also touches on slavery, the devshirme system and the debate over Sinan's origins. The demolition of Taqi al-Din's observatory in 1580 becomes an example of how science is sacrificed in religious and court politics.
His conclusion is that through buildings, Shafak shows that stones hold on to the hopes, struggles and memories of their time.
nazar: Speaking about the Armenian massacres is still a risk in Turkey. In India too there is a trend of removing uncomfortable chapters of history from the syllabus, so this reading is not a distant matter for us.
The episode of the observatory's demolition reminds us that when power and faith decide together, the first to be sacrificed is the knowledge that asks questions.
sawal: How long can a society escape the history it has forgotten?
ref: Mimar Sinan
The sixteenth-century Ottoman architect who built hundreds of buildings, including the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul.
Devshirme
The Ottoman Empire's practice of taking boys from Christian families and training them for the army and administration.
photo_note: Sultan Suleiman on a hunt, a miniature from the Süleymanname

h: Vijayadashami's festival, Hudur Durga's mourning
dek: In Hindwi Bela's series 'C/O Bengal', Baby Shaw writes that in the same myth through which Bengal celebrates victory, the Santals and other Adivasis remember the defeat of their ancestor.
body: Baby Shaw's article opens in the mood of the farewell of Durga Puja: the sound of the dhak (drum), sindoor khela (women smearing vermilion on each other), preparations for immersing the idol. In the crowd, a boy playfully stuffs a big rasgulla into the asura's mouth and people laugh. But Dhodru Panna, standing nearby, finds no fun in it, because for him that asura is a memory of ancestors and a mark of a lost history. The writer finds him like a character standing apart in Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay's 'Aranyak' (Of the Forest).

The article's central argument is that the same myth can be a celebration for some and a mourning for others. It first recalls the story in the Puranas and then two traditions of the Ramayana: in Valmiki, Rama worships the Sun before battle, while in the fifteenth-century Krittivasi Ramayana, Durga's akal bodhan (untimely invocation) takes place in autumn.

Among the Santals and other Adivasi communities of Jharkhand and Bengal's Jangalmahal, Mahishasura is remembered as Hudur Durga. In the folk tale the writer mentions, Hudur Durga was the just king of Chaichampa, whose fertile land was resented by outsiders. Through deceit a woman was placed before him, and the king laid down his arms because Santal custom does not allow striking a woman. That is why this death is called not a battle but a murder.

According to the writer, people never accepted his death, and from this belief came the Dasai dance, performed in many districts of Bengal and Jharkhand. In some villages, no lamp is lit and no meat is cooked during the days of the puja. She believes the mainstream ignores this story, even though it is an important part of the politics of Dalit and Adivasi identity.
Her conclusion is that Indian culture is not imprisoned in any one religious story, and that respecting the different meanings of the same festival is its real strength.
nazar: In recent years, speaking about the Adivasi memory of Mahishasura has become a cause of controversy, and in some places even of court cases. So it matters that this article has appeared on a mainstream literary website.
The insistence on tying a festival to a single meaning makes strangers of the communities for whom those same days are days of mourning. Plurality means making room for the other's memory too.
sawal: Can one festival make room for two different memories?
ref: Dasai
A dance of the Santals and other Adivasi communities, performed around Durga Puja in memory of Hudur Durga.
Akal bodhan
Untimely worship. The story in the Krittivasi Ramayana in which Rama awakens Durga in autumn; Bengal's Durga Puja is linked to it.

h: A continent of six seasons, and our fading memory
dek: On Janakipul, Tribhuvan writes that the subcontinent's understanding of six seasons lived in language, raga and farming, and colonial education squeezed it into three or four.
body: This article by Tribhuvan, a journalist and writer from Jaipur, grew out of a social media exchange. Janakipul's editor Prabhat Ranjan wrote something about sharad (autumn), Tribhuvan replied that hemant (early winter) had already arrived, and then years-old notes were quickly polished into this article.

His core argument is that the subcontinent divided the year into six seasons: vasant, grishma, varsha, sharad, hemant and shishir (spring, summer, rains, autumn, early winter and late winter). This division came from close watching of nature and a fine vocabulary of feelings. According to the writer, colonial education and modern meteorology cut it down to three or four seasons, and local understanding kept vanishing from books. The Vedic texts mention three, five and six seasons, which means this system took shape gradually alongside farming and geography.

The article sets out on a journey through languages. It mentions the Rajasthani poet Chandra Singh Birkali's 'Badli' (Little Cloud) and 'Lu' (Hot Wind), and also that Rajasthani has more than forty words for rain. Herders in western Rajasthan sense rain before the clouds appear. The season traditions of Arabic, Persian, Urdu, Punjabi, Nepali, Tamil, Kashmiri and Bangla also come into view.

Discussing Kalidasa's 'Ritusamhara' (The Gathering of Seasons) and 'Meghaduta' (The Cloud Messenger), Tribhuvan also says that classical descriptions of the seasons are mostly through the eyes of male poets and need to be reread from women's point of view. Barahmasa folk songs, Jayasi, the ragas Hindol and Megh, Ayurveda's ritucharya (seasonal routine) and Iran's Gahambar festivals also join this map.
In the end he links the changing seasons to the climate crisis and, recalling the record hot year of 2024, says the seasons will not return on their own; nature will have to be saved.
nazar: This article reminds us that knowledge of the weather is stored not only in satellites but also in herders, farmers and folk songs, and that this knowledge lies first with the people on the margins.
Tribhuvan's point that the season culture of Punjab, Bengal and Kashmir does not respect political borders is also important. In a time of climate crisis, this shared heritage is also a shared worry.
sawal: How many days does hemant last in your area now?
ref: Hemant
The season after sharad and before shishir, roughly the months of Kartik and Aghan, when a light chill begins.
Barahmasa
A form of folk and devotional poetry that describes the twelve months of the year, often with a feeling of longing for an absent beloved.
